title: Buying a Home From Out of State: A Practical Guide
description: Buying a home from out of state in Middle Tennessee? Learn how virtual tours, market numbers, inspections and closing steps work before you relocate.
keyword: buying a home from out of state
body:
Moving to Middle Tennessee for work or family often means shopping for a house you cannot walk through whenever you like. Buying a home from out of state is common, and it gets easier when you break it into pieces: the money, the market, the home itself, and the move. Here is how I walk through each one.

## Get the money side clear first

{{img:0}}

Before you spend hours on listings, find out what you can borrow. Pre-approval is different from pre-qualification. Pre-approval means a lender has reviewed your documents, so ask for that before you get serious about a specific home.

Rates change often, so treat any number as a snapshot. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, according to Freddie Mac via FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. You can plug your own numbers into the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator) to see how a rate changes a monthly payment.

Price is only part of the cash you need. Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. Down payment rules depend on the loan type:

- FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent.
- VA loans typically require no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee may apply.
- Conventional loans typically require private mortgage insurance when the down payment is under 20 percent.

A lender can tell you which of these fits your situation. The [CFPB Owning a Home guides](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) explain the loan process in plain language.

One more point that matters for relocations. From the time you apply for a loan through closing, avoid opening new credit, financing furniture, or changing jobs. If a job change is part of your move, talk with your lender about timing first.

## Read the local market before you pick a town

Middle Tennessee is not one market. Prices and pace shift from town to town, so it helps to look at a few side by side.

In Franklin, the median sale price was $862,929 as of 2026-08-31, up 12.4% from a year earlier, with a median of 49 days on market and 3.6 months of supply (Redfin, rolling 3 months). In Spring Hill, the median sale price was $508,284, down 4.1% from a year earlier, with 62 median days on market and 4.1 months of supply (same source and date). For the wider Nashville metro, Redfin reported a median sale price of $461,491, 68 median days on market and 5.6 months of supply for the 4 weeks ending 2026-09-27.

Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers. By that measure, Franklin sits just under the line at 3.6 months, while Spring Hill and the Nashville metro land in the balanced range. Zillow's index shows cooling in all three over the last 3 months. These are descriptions of recent data, not predictions.

Geography can trip up newcomers too. Spring Hill includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties, so county services, schools and taxes can differ by address. Murfreesboro is in Rutherford County and Columbia is in Maury County. Neither is in Williamson County. For more detail, see the [market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data), the [Franklin area guide](/areas/franklin) and the [Spring Hill area guide](/areas/spring-hill).

## Tour a home you cannot stand in

{{img:1}}

Virtual tours and video walkthroughs are useful for layout, condition and light. They do not show everything. Ask your agent for a live video walkthrough where you can direct the camera, plus video of the street and surroundings. Ask to see the parts that listing photos often skip, like the garage, attic access, crawl space and the yard.

Then lean on paperwork. Tennessee sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure (or an exemption), and the lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. Read both closely and ask questions about anything unclear.

Inspections matter even more when you cannot be there. Termite and wood-destroying organism (WDO) inspections are commonly requested by buyers and lenders in Tennessee. Radon testing, a sewer scope and a termite inspection are common add-ons to a standard home inspection. The [EPA radon information](https://www.epa.gov/radon) page explains what radon is and how testing works. If you can attend the inspection by video, do.

Schools and taxes need a separate check. School assignment and property taxes depend on the exact address. For any home you are serious about, verify assignment with [Williamson County Schools](https://www.wcs.edu) or the district that covers the address, and look up the parcel through the [Williamson County property search](https://www.williamsoncounty-tn.gov/2099/35739/Property-Data-Search) or the correct county office.

Commutes are worth testing yourself. Pull up [TDOT SmartWay traffic](https://smartway.tn.gov) and check the route at the hours you would actually drive. If you can make even one trip before closing, use it to drive that route and see the area at different times of day.

## Plan the closing and the move

Distance adds a few risks, and most of them are manageable.

- **Closing Disclosure.** A lender must send it at least 3 business days before closing. Compare it with your Loan Estimate and ask about any difference.
- **Wire fraud.** It is real. Verify wire instructions by phone using a number you already trust, and never rely on emailed wire instructions.
- **Movers.** Request quotes from at least 3 licensed moving companies and book early for month-end dates.
- **Insurance on your old home.** Cancel homeowner's insurance on a sold home only after closing is confirmed.

I keep [moving checklists](/checklists) on this site that cover the steps above in order, so you can work through them at your own pace.

## Your next step

If you are planning a move to Middle Tennessee and want to talk it through, use the [Get Matched form](/buy#form). Scott schedules a call, and you will be talking within the next 48 hours. You can also [contact Scott](/contact) directly with questions. If you are selling a home elsewhere, you can start with the [home value request](/sell#form) on this site, and a local agent where you live can help with that side of the move.

faq.q: Can you buy a home without seeing it in person?
faq.a: Yes, many buyers do. Live video walkthroughs, the seller's disclosures and inspections help fill the gap. If you can make one trip before closing, use it to see the home and the surrounding area.

faq.q: What is the difference between pre-approval and pre-qualification?
faq.a: Pre-approval means a lender has reviewed your documents. Pre-qualification is a different, earlier step. A lender can explain what each one means for your loan.

faq.q: How much cash do I need beyond the down payment?
faq.a: Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent, and VA loans typically require no down payment.

faq.q: How do I avoid wire fraud when closing from far away?
faq.a: Verify wire instructions by phone using a number you already trust. Never rely on wire instructions sent by email.

faq.q: How do I find out which school or tax rate applies to a home?
faq.a: Both depend on the exact address. Verify school assignment with the school district and property taxes with the county for any home you are serious about.
